 Should Daylight Saving Time be made permanent? 
 WILLIAM PATRICK PAINE
william.paine@thecarrollnews.com

 Lately, there has been a concerted effort to make Daylight Saving Time permanent. The Carroll News took a random poll to find out what our readers think of this idea.
 Daylight saving time advances the clock one hour so that the sun sets one hour later in the afternoon but conversely rises 1 hour later in the morning. Under Daylight Saving Time, when the sun reaches the apex of its arc in the sky at noon, the artificially advanced clock does not read 12p.m. but instead registers as 1p.m.
 In recent years, Daylight Saving has been extended so that it starts earlier and ends later than in the past. This year, Daylight Saving Time went into effect on Sunday March 8, and is set to go back to Standard Time on Sunday November 1.
 If Daylight Saving was made permanent, there would be an extra hour of sunlight in mid winter but the sun would rise notably later in the morning. As it stands now, on December 21, in Hillsville, the sun will rise at 7:31a.m. and set at 5:09. Daylight Saving would push this to an 8:31a.m. sunrise and a 6:09p.m. sunset.
 Here is the Poll Question:
 Should the United States adopt Daylight Saving permanently?
 Or
 Should the United States return to Standard Time?
 Or
 Should the United States continue with the annual Spring Ahead/Fall Back regimen?
 Alicia Fain and Ariel Caldwell were on their lunch break walk when the Carroll News caught up with them.
 “They should make it permanent,” Fain declared. “100 percent!”
 “A million percent!,” added Ariel Caldwell.
 “Because in the evenings after you get off work, you can do stuff and you don’t feel like it’s so draggy,” said Fain.
 “I agree,” Caldwell added. “And people who work later jobs, you know, not getting off in the dark.”
 “Because you’re gonna get up and go to work anyway,” Fain continued. “It’s not like you can do anything in the morning.”
 “I’m old school,” said Lynn Holdaway, as she raked the lawn. “I remember my mother always said, ‘Spring forward, fall back.’ I’d rather keep it how it’s been.”
 “Best to keep it the same,” remarked Landon Shupe, as he entered his N. Main Street apartment building in Hillsville.
 “It’s probably better staying like it is because it would be dark until 8 o’clock in the morning,” said John Carter at a school board meeting. “It’s probably safer for the kids with the school busses.”
 The guys in the barber shop had a different view.
 “I think permanent is the way I’d go,” said Ray Larussa. “This nonsense of switching it back, you know, twice a year is ridiculous. As far as late sunrises. That’s all right. I like to sleep in!”
 “Yes make it permanent,” declared Ross Lishen. “One, it simplifies it. You don’t go through the change. Two, I’d rather have more daylight in the evening when I get off work. I got more time to get something done, even in the winter. That’s the big deal to me because at night you get off in the winter time, you don’t have any time to get something done before the sun goes down. If the sun comes up later, you’re going to be going to work anyway.”
 “Yeah,” said Kenneth Hensley. “I’d like for it to stay the same all the time year round.”
 “You’ll get used to it,” agreed Marion Wade. “I think your body feels better.”
 “I’m in favor of it, too,” added Kenny Wurzburger. “Simply because the Democrats is against it.”
 “I think you just need leave it alone,” said Scott Marshall in his dissent. “Keep it like it is.”
 “My emotions are split because I would love for it to be permanent but at the same time, I’m afraid of it being dark when the kids go to school in the morning,” said Greg Crowder, as he tended to town business. “So I think it should stay the same as it is now.”
 “My first choice would be to keep the system we have now,” said Shelby Puckett between showing visitors around the J. Sidna Allen House. “My second my second choice would be to go to standard time all the time.”
 “I’m in favor of a permanent daylight saving time because I don’t want it to get dark out at 4:30 in the afternoon,” said Ryan McCafferty, as he penned his latest sports story. “Darker mornings don’t bother me because I’m not a huge morning person.”
 The following individuals responded to the daylight saving questions via email.
 “I prefer standard time, or the current schedule,” wrote Naomi Hall. “It seems like the night owls are most interested in permanent daylight savings time.”
 “I say continue as we have with the annual spring ahead/fall back,-:)”,responded Lindsey Edmonds.
 “Personally, I would prefer returning to Standard Time permanently,” wrote Dwayne Huff. “I believe there would be biological and health benefits to this practice. Research continues to show the benefits of getting a good night’s sleep and staying with Standard Time promotes natural circadian rhythms and better sleep habits. As a school administrator, I would also favor this option. Students with good sleep habits typically perform better. It is also hard to imagine the school day starting at 8:00 am and it would still be dark outside if Daylight Saving Time was year round. While the longer summer days are often nice for recreational activities and help some businesses, I don’t think it is worth the negative impacts it has on our health.”
